prompt: Is it better to have a few close friends or many casual ones? Write an essay with a clear position.
text:
# Why a Few Close Friends Beat Many Casual Ones

If I had to choose between a small circle of close friends and a large network of casual ones, I would choose the small circle. Casual friends make life more pleasant. Close friends make it more bearable and more meaningful. When the two compete for limited time and energy, depth should win.

The strongest argument for close friends is what they do for us in hard times. When you lose a job, face an illness, or go through a divorce, you do not call someone you see twice a year at parties. You call the person who already knows your history and who will pick up at midnight. Casual friends tend to offer sympathy. Close friends offer help, such as a spare room, a ride to the hospital, or a hard truth you need to hear. That kind of support depends on trust, and trust takes years of shared time to build.

Close friendship also changes how well we are known. With a casual friend, we show a polished version of ourselves. We talk about work, weather, and weekend plans. With a close friend, we can admit fear, confusion, or failure and still be accepted. Being known this way is one of the deepest human needs. Without it, a person can be surrounded by acquaintances and still feel lonely. Loneliness is not a shortage of contacts. It is a shortage of connection.

Time is the other reason. Friendship takes hours, and each of us has only so many. Researchers who study social groups, most famously the anthropologist Robin Dunbar, have found that people have only a handful of relationships at the closest level, and that each additional person dilutes the attention the others receive. If we spread ourselves across fifty casual friendships, we may have too little left for the few that could matter most. Depth is expensive, so it has to be chosen on purpose.

The best case for casual friends deserves a fair hearing. Wide networks bring new ideas, job leads, and introductions that a tight circle cannot. Sociologists call these "weak ties," and they are often how people find opportunities. Casual friends also make daily life warmer, through the friendly neighbor, the gym regular, or the coworker who jokes at the coffee machine. These bonds are real, and they add up to a sense of belonging.

But this argument shows that casual friends are useful, not that they should come first. Weak ties need very little from us. A greeting, a quick chat, or an occasional message keeps them alive. Because they are cheap to maintain, we can have them alongside close friends without much sacrifice. Close friendships cannot be kept up that way. They are what we lose if we do not protect them. So the real choice is not between the two kinds. It is about where to put our best effort, and the answer is the people who would show up for us.

A good life probably includes both: a few deep friendships at the center and a looser circle around them. But if one must come first, it should be the close friends. They are the ones who know us, stand by us, and remain when everything else changes. A crowded address book is pleasant, but a few people who truly know you are worth more.
